text: An archivist annotates the brittle edge of a paper tape in pencil: Unsolved cases, too, must be preserved as they are, never overwritten.
What Became of the Recipients
Some still need follow-up care. The hard-won technical records never made up for the harm suffered when the signal was received.
The sealed underground shelter doors are still swept of snow and rust each day by ordinary surface patrols. The silence in the tunnels does not mean that tragedy never came to pass.
Under pressure, the historical inquiry team refused to stitch together the conflicting fragments of wartime records into a logically consistent “definitive order” by sheer invention.
The archive ends with the mud and scorched earth of the surface. It will never invent a supernatural shortcut to salvation for the community rebuilding here.
Another Star on the Chart
On the rusted dispatch board in the freight yard, the faded destination still reads “Mars.”
Before the flames consumed the ionosphere, that was the route chart generations of pioneers followed to venture from home or return with honor.
The Weather Before the Evacuation
The last string of clear text on the punched tape read: Orbital supplies cut off. Everyone evacuate.
The surviving logs recovered from shelters across the region are filled with suffocating accounts of the sky's orbital supply lines failing completely.

The sealed files of opposing factions give sharply conflicting accounts of who broke the agreement first. Here among the ruins, no yellowed document deserves to serve as the final testimony condemning all those who died in vain.
The First Message Sent Out
The antenna at the new tracking station turned slowly, pointing toward the dark sky.

The transmission pierced the ionosphere. Its first message carried only a surface peace call and coordinates for safe near-Earth routes, with no words of judgment or declaration of revenge. Whether any survivors are still listening from the dark depths of space remains unconfirmed.
A Flight That Began on the Ground

The chief engineer spread out rough recycled graph paper and carefully drew the water lines and geothermal power grid of the lowland settlement alongside the escape and return trajectories of near-Earth orbiters, all on one blueprint.
Escaping the surface's gravity does not erase responsibility for the ruins below.
Before the Hatch Closes
The sealed-cabin test log lists water, food, air filters, emergency injections, and spare parts in detail.
Every gram of supplies came from the actual labor of ground workshops; every loss of cabin pressure was recorded with the person responsible and the cause.
Beyond the Porthole
The crew's faces appeared behind three layers of pressure-resistant glass. The underground settlement kept their beds and places on the rolls ready for their return.
The uncrewed probe had no heartbeat. The telemetry it sent back to the surface waited in silence for the people who would truly board a ship someday.
This journey into near-Earth orbit ended with nothing more than the gentle opening of an unlocked door on the surface of this scarred planet.
A Few More Pairs of Shoes
At last, through the long frozen nights, someone took turns tending the fire by the hearth.
Not one muddy pair of shoes by the door fit well. Their soles were worn and patchy, but they belonged to people who had survived.
Tomorrow morning's rations need weighing again. The wooden bed in the corner stands empty; who knows who may arrive in the night.
From Names to Addresses
The first permanent street sign, hammered from scrap metal, went up at the muddy crossroads.
Messages and delivery slips could now be sent to specific places, instead of relying on chance and calling someone's name in a crowd.
The commitments demanded by literacy classes at night school, shelter clinics, and leveled dirt roads last far longer than making do with a single dinner.
The Forest Is No Longer All You See
The first neighborhood census sheets were neatly bound into a thin booklet with coarse hemp twine.
The drained fields and foundry workshops each had shift schedules. Purified water and anti-inflammatory medicine could no longer be rationed only for the original residents.
You began deciding who would receive new capabilities first, and who would have to wait.
Morning in Another City
A convoy unloaded cargo crates stamped with unfamiliar seals from elsewhere.
Some brought repair bills stained with machine oil; others carried a carefully worded proposal for a joint alliance council.

For the first time, the region's public ledger faced a pointed question: Why were expenses charged to this city in full, while supplies were sent to a foreign community a hundred miles away for their use first?
One Ledger of Daily Life
Some chose new joints; others kept their original bodies.
Hydroponic gardens and precision lathes coexist in the same neighborhood, each in its place.
Technological change never had the right to decide how anyone should live. But it forced civilization to draw the boundaries of one another's rights more clearly, line by line.
The Weather on the Far Side of the Sea
Radio call signs from every major region were entered into the same global watch roster, one by one according to schedule.
Every settlement still bore the deep scars, dialects, and stubborn habits shaped by its own ordeal.
The common code learned to chart routes across oceans, and to stop with restraint before knocking on someone else's door.
